summary: Proposes Early Retransmit for TCP and SCTP, which lowers the number of duplicate acknowledgments needed to trigger fast retransmit when the congestion window is small. This lets lost segments be repaired without waiting for a long timeout. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: If only a few things are in flight and one goes missing, you ask for it again after fewer reminders instead of waiting a long time.

subtitle: Faster recovery from packet loss when the send window is small

tldr.problem: When TCP or SCTP has a small congestion window (fewer than 4 segments in flight), a single lost packet cannot generate enough duplicate acknowledgments to trigger fast retransmit, forcing the sender to wait for a costly timeout (minimum 1 second).
tldr.mechanism: Early Retransmit reduces the duplicate acknowledgment threshold when certain conditions hold: the amount of outstanding data is small, and no new data is available for transmission. Two variants are proposed: byte-based (checks outstanding bytes) and segment-based (counts segments).
tldr.outcome: Short connections and connections at the end of data transfer can recover from loss quickly via fast retransmit instead of waiting for the retransmission timeout, improving overall performance.

today: RFC 5827 is an Experimental specification, published for evaluation and potential future standards adoption. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The specification remains as a reference for implementations exploring improved loss recovery for connections with small congestion windows.

sections.title: The Small Window Problem
sections.content: Standard TCP and SCTP have two mechanisms to recover from packet loss. The first is a retransmission timeout (RTO): if an acknowledgment does not arrive within a timeout period, the sender resends the oldest unacknowledged data. The second is fast retransmit: when three duplicate acknowledgments arrive, indicating that a packet was lost, the sender resends the lost packet immediately without waiting for the timeout. However, fast retransmit requires that enough packets be in flight to generate three duplicate acknowledgments when one is lost. When the congestion window is small—fewer than four segments—fast retransmit cannot trigger because the receiver cannot generate three duplicate acknowledgments from the remaining in-flight packets. This happens frequently at the start of a connection during slow-start, near the end of a transfer when data runs out, or for connections limited by the receiver's advertised window. Because the minimum RTO is conservatively set to one second to avoid spurious retransmissions of delayed packets, a single lost segment at the end of a transfer can add a full second of latency.
sections.eli5: Normally you need three 'I didn't get it' messages to ask for a resend. But if you only sent three things total and one was lost, you can't get three complaints.

sections.title: The Early Retransmit Algorithm
sections.content: Early Retransmit allows the sender to use fast retransmit with a lower duplicate acknowledgment threshold when two conditions are met: (1) the amount of outstanding data is small, and (2) the sender has no unsent data available or the receiver's window does not permit sending more data. When these conditions hold, the sender can retransmit a lost segment after receiving fewer duplicate acknowledgments. The RFC specifies two variants. The byte-based variant checks if outstanding bytes are less than 4 times the maximum segment size (SMSS). It uses the formula ER_thresh = ceiling(ownd/SMSS) - 1 to determine the threshold. For example, if there are 1200 bytes outstanding with an SMSS of 1460 bytes, the threshold becomes zero, meaning any duplicate ACK can trigger retransmit. The segment-based variant counts the actual number of outstanding segments. It triggers when fewer than four segments are in flight, using the formula ER_thresh = oseg - 1. For example, with two segments in flight, the sender retransmits after one duplicate ACK. The segment-based variant is more precise but requires tracking segment boundaries.
sections.eli5: When you only have a couple of things in flight, lower the bar from 'three complaints' to 'just one complaint'.

sections.title: SACK-Based and Non-SACK Variants
sections.content: The RFC provides both SACK and non-SACK versions for TCP. SACK (Selective Acknowledgment) allows the receiver to tell the sender exactly which packets have been received, not just the highest contiguous sequence number. The SACK-based variant of Early Retransmit is preferred in TCP because it is more robust to ACK loss. With SACK, the sender looks for explicit information that one or more segments have been acknowledged (SACKed) in addition to checking the duplicate ACK count. Specifically, with SACK, Early Retransmit triggers only when ownd - SMSS bytes (or oseg - 1 segments) have been SACKed. This gives the sender confidence that a segment is truly lost rather than merely reordered. The non-SACK variant is available for older TCP implementations or connections that do not negotiate SACK, but it is less robust to reordering and delayed acknowledgments. SCTP always uses a SACK-like mechanism and naturally uses the SACK-based variant.
sections.eli5: With SACK, the receiver says exactly which packets arrived, so you're more confident something is really lost rather than just late.

sections.title: Risks and Trade-Offs
sections.content: Early Retransmit improves recovery speed at the cost of reduced robustness to segment reordering. If the network reorders packets, the sender might see a duplicate ACK and mistakenly believe a packet is lost when it has merely been delayed. Research shows that reducing the duplicate ACK threshold from three to two (without the other conditions) increases spurious retransmissions threefold. Early Retransmit includes the additional condition that the window must be small, but reordering in the context of small windows remains a concern. Worst-case scenarios can occur: persistent reordering combined with applications that send data in small bursts can result in unnecessary retransmissions. For example, an application sending two segments at a time, if consistently reordered, will retransmit one segment unnecessarily every other burst. However, the document notes these cases are likely pathological. The RFC does not mandate Early Retransmit but leaves adoption to implementers, and treats this as an Experimental specification for evaluation before potential standardization.
sections.eli5: If packets sometimes come out of order on the network, Early Retransmit might send too many copies. But in real networks with small windows, this is rare.

cells: Less precise; poor for small payloads

items.title: When to use
items.text: Small window AND no new data available

items.title: Benefit
items.text: Avoid 1-second RTO at end of transfers

items.title: Risk
items.text: More spurious retransmits on reordered networks

items.title: SACK advantage
items.text: More confident segment is truly lost, not delayed
